title: The Puddle
summary:
In a talk in 1998, Douglas Adams said: "This is rather as if you imagine a puddle waking up one morning and thinking, 'This is an interesting world I find myself in - an interesting hole I find myself in - fits me rather neatly, doesn't it? In fact it fits me staggeringly well, must have been made to have me in it!'" As the sun rises and the puddle shrinks, it goes on hanging on to the idea that everything will be all right, because the world was made to have it in it; so the moment it disappears catches it rather by surprise.

The joke is aimed at the argument from fine-tuning: that the laws and constants of physics seem to be just right for life, so they must have been set that way for us. It makes the anthropic point: of course we find ourselves in a world that suits us, since we could only have come about in one that did. We took the world's shape, not it ours. Defenders of fine-tuning reply that this still doesn't explain why there is a life-permitting world at all.
